title: Formalizing invertebrate cryptic species descriptions: clarifying a pragmatic DNA-based and stable nomenclatural framework
abstract: consistent with the ICZN and allowing for the formal description of lineages without the absolute requirement of DNA from historical types. The present Opinion follows the publication of the Comment by Davinack and Fitzhugh (2026) as well as other feedback received in response to our paper (Vivien et al., 2025). In light of these various comments, we wish to reaffirm our original recommendations and address the conceptual and methodological concerns raised, several of which stem from a misunderstanding or a misrepresentation of our approach. These criticisms span all aspects of our proposal-from nomenclatural compliance and type preservation to the reliability of molecular data and the status of historical types. We address each point below by providing further evidence and formal clarifications. A comparison of the taxonomic recommendations for the description of invertebrate cryptic species, highlighting both points of consensus and divergence between Vivien et al. (2025) and subsequent commentaries (e.g., Davinack & Fitzhugh, 2026), is provided in Table 1. Contrary to the opinion of Davinack and Fitzhugh (2026), our aim is neither to equate all genetic divergence with species status nor to circumvent the Code, but to propose a taxonomic practice adapted to cryptic diversity, based on explicit diagnostic characters and nomenclatural stability. This approach is particularly relevant given the inherent limitations of traditional morphology in resolving many invertebrate complexes and the rise of molecular data as an independent and essential source of characters. By formalizing these lineages, we ensure their integration into scientific and conservation frameworks as traceable taxonomic units rather than ephemeral informal labels. [Insert Table 1 here].To address the assertion by Davinack and Fitzhugh (2026) and other commentators that molecular data alone are insufficient for species delimitation, we here clarify the robust nature of genetic evidence-a level of detail that was not fully developed in our original proposal. Rather than providing mere suggestions, various analytic methods have been developed to formally assess whether genetic lineages correspond to independently evolving metapopulations, in accordance with de Queiroz's unified concept of species (de Queiroz, 2007). Distance-based approaches (ABGD, ASAP), coalescence (KoT), phylogenetic trees (PTP) or speciation models (GMYC) (Pons et al., 2006;Puillandre et al., 2021;Puillandre et al., 2012;Spöri et al., 2021;Zhang et al., 2013) offer rigorous and complementary tools for formulating explicit, reproducible, and revisable species hypotheses. Lineages are identified based on robust genetic differences and evaluated using multiple markers whenever possible. This framework ensures that species hypotheses are verifiable and traceable, allowing cryptic biodiversity to be rapidly documented without sacrificing scientific rigour.Contrary to Davinack & Fitzhugh (2026), our initial Opinion did not dismiss integrative taxonomy; rather, it reconciled this ideal with the practical constraints of cryptic species discovery. While a multi-evidence approach is desirable, its universal application is frequently hindered by significant operational limitations. By definition, cryptic lineages lack clear diagnostic characters; any morphological differences are typically subtle, overlapping, or too ambiguous to allow for reliable species delimitation. Likewise, behavioural or reproductive experiments are feasible for only a small fraction of taxa. Similarly, integrating ecological data requires extensive sampling across multiple locations-a task often rendered impossible by the low abundance and patchy distribution typical of many invertebrate species. Furthermore, phenotypic traits are often inconclusive due to plasticity (risk of over-delimitation) or niche conservatism (masking distinct lineages). Shared ecological or behavioural preferences may thus not reliably indicate conspecificity, offering lower resolution than molecular evidence. We adopt a realist interpretation of species consistent with the unified species concept of de Queiroz (2007), under which species correspond to separately evolving metapopulation lineages. Within this framework, species are treated as real historical entities, while diagnostic criteria serve as operational tools for their inference. Importantly, as species boundaries are not directly observable, we contend that molecular diagnosability provides a primary and sufficient line of evidence for inferring lineage independence, especially when morphological signals are limited. In this light, our proposal focuses on the formulation of robust species hypotheses, validated by molecular evidence and ready for formal description. This reflects a pragmatic response to empirical constraints rather than a reduction of species recognition to a single data source, providing a workable alternative where traditional phenotypic diagnostic approaches are often impracticable. Davinack & Fitzhugh (2026) mandate testing additional hypotheses, such as population structure or isolation by distance. While valuable, these lack clear species-delimitation thresholds and require intensive geographical sampling that is frequently impractical. By imposing such requirements without a workable methodological framework, their stance risks maintaining a status quo that hinders taxonomic progress. Beyond these biological constraints, while we strongly support the acquisition of additional data to refine and further test molecularly identified lineages, their mandatory inclusion for formal description remains problematic. A major challenge is the lack of consensus on how to prioritize and weight different evidence types, often leading to inconsistent delimitation standards. We argue that when molecular markers are proven robust for a given group, they provide a sufficient and objective basis for formal description. Requiring further evidence-in the absence of a clear and objective methodology to arbitrate between data types-merely introduces a layer of subjectivity into the taxonomic process. As discussed above, these multiple lines of evidence are often impossible to acquire or may prove uninformative. In such cases, DNA sequences may represent the only operationally accessible source of evidence sufficiently informative for species delimitation. Systematically requiring additional, independent data types when they are unavailable inevitably delays or prevents the formal description of a significant portion of invertebrate diversity. Historically, taxonomic descriptions have been based primarily on morphological evidence; our proposal simply advocates for a similar pragmatic standard in the molecular era, ensuring that the formal naming of life can still proceed with rigour even when only genetic data are available. We acknowledge that molecular data may occasionally prove inconclusive-for instance, when genetic divergence is near established thresholds or when markers show incongruence. In such ambiguous cases, we advocate for treating species hypotheses as provisional, requiring the acquisition of further genomic data and, where possible, complementary evidence to achieve a decisive delimitation.In cases where only molecular data are accessible, Davinack & Fitzhugh (2026) advocate for a status quo, where cryptic diversity remains relegated to informal labels in public databases, pending the potential-yet uncertain-availability of additional evidence. However, the proliferation of such codes (BINs, OTUs, MOTUs, etc.) represents a major obstacle for biodiversity management. As noted by Horton et al. (2025), this accumulation of informal names in public databases creates a significant tracking challenge and an urgent need for standardized solutions. Currently, determining whether different identifiers linked to a single morphospecies represent the same biological entity requires complex, group-specific phylogenetic analyses. While useful for structuring genetic data, these provisional codes lack the nomenclatural status necessary for sustainable integration into conservation frameworks (Delić et al., 2017;Samyn and De Clerck, 2012). Our approach directly addresses this gap by formalising these validated candidates into named species. By transforming informal labels into formal taxa, we replace technical ambiguity with a stable name, ensuring consistent identification across studies. 5. Historical names, types, species inquirendae and nomina dubia Some critics misrepresented our guidelines for managing legacy nomenclature. First, as stated in our proposal, cryptic lineages may be formally described without prior attribution of a particular lineage to a historical type only when the type material is not traceable after reasonable effort, may be unsuitable for genetic analysis, or when a neotype cannot readily be designated. If a type cannot be reliably compared with newly identified molecular units, conspecificity cannot be demonstrated at the time of description. In such cases, the nominal taxon is best regarded as species inquirenda, and the specific status assigned to newly named lineages must be treated as a revisable species-level hypothesis. This remains subject to future revision should further evidence allow the unambiguous association of a lineage with an existing historical name or lead to a refined delimitation. Second, historical names may be treated as nomina dubia only when it is demonstrably impossible to associate them with a biological entity because the type material is missing, degraded, non-diagnostic, or unsuitable for modern genetic analyses, or when the type locality is imprecise or unknown. The use of nomen dubium is therefore necessary to maintain nomenclatural stability and prevent the arbitrary assignment of names. Although the Code does not require prior assignment of newly identified lineages to historical types as a precondition for valid description, some authors argue that such assignment should be methodologically mandatory. If strictly enforced, this requirement would effectively preclude the formal recognition of many cryptic lineages whenever the original material suffers from the aforementioned limitations. Imposing such a constraint would substantially impede the description of cryptic diversity, as a vast number of historical names are based on such problematic material. 6. Synonymy, stability and revisability Some commentators have argued that describing lineages without prior attribution to a historical type should be avoided, fearing that it will lead to an increase in junior synonyms and significant nomenclatural instability. Specifically, this risk arises if formally described cryptic lineages are subsequently shown to correspond to historical types-a predictable consequence of nomenclature based on partial knowledge, also well-known in morphological taxonomy. When documented transparently, these revisions do not undermine the nomenclature. Once a lineage is unambiguously linked to a historical type, the original name followed by "sensu stricto" can be used consistently, ensuring stability, clarity and reproducibility of identifications while limiting the risk of confusion. While the creation of junior synonyms remains a possibility, we argue that the benefits of our approach -namely improved lineage traceability, consistent use of phylogenetic units, and reduced taxonomic ambiguity -far outweigh these potential nomenclatural drawbacks.In our initial proposal, we recommended characterizing each newly described cryptic species at least to the morphospecies level. While some commentators have recommended including exhaustive morphological descriptions for all new taxa, such a requirement prior to naming hinders the documentation of many cryptic species. Fully mature specimens are rare for taxa that are uncommon or difficult to collect, and some groups are never or very rarely encountered in a state that allows for complete morphological characterisation (e.g., Chaetogaster) (Vivien et al., 2024). Our approach does not exclude exhaustive morphological study when required expertise and optimal specimens-displaying the full suite of morphological characters necessary for fine-scale species delimitation-are available. However, by enabling rapid and formal recognition of cryptic species, it creates a framework in which subsequent morphological, ecological, or behavioural analyses can be conducted efficiently, without detracting from existing expertise. In this context, Davinack & Fitzhugh (2026) and other commentators seem to have implicitly criticised our approach for not linking cryptic lineages to type material that is morphologically identifiable at the lineage level. Yet, as we have emphasized, providing such morphologically diagnostic vouchers is by definition practically impossible at the time of description. Nonetheless, even when morphological data are currently inconclusive, the preservation of these specimens remains essential. While they may not permit lineage identification today, the rapid development of new tools-such as artificial intelligence and high-resolution 3D imaging-will likely render these vouchers informative in the future.Article 13.1.1 of the ICZN (1999) requires that a new species name include a description differentiating the taxon; it does not limit characters to morphology. Molecular diagnoses are thus fully compatible with the Code. Methods such as CAOS, UITOTO and MoID can be used to identify diagnostic molecular characters for formulating formal molecular diagnoses (Fedosov et al., 2022;Sarkar et al., 2008;Torres et al., 2025). In line with our original proposal, we insist that each newly described cryptic species must be supported by such a molecular diagnosis and the designation of physical type material preserved in public institutions to ensure accessibility, verifiability, and long-term stability. We therefore reject the assertion by Davinack & Fitzhugh (2026) and other commentators that our approach weakens ICZN standards or overlooks the necessity of vouchers.The formal naming of cryptic invertebrates necessitates: (1) explicitly stated, reproducible species-delimitation criteria; (2) the recognition of taxonomic hypotheses as inherently revisable; and (3) robust methodologies for generating reliable molecular diagnoses. Davinack and Fitzhugh (2026) advocate for increased investment in museum collections and morphological taxonomy training as a primary solution. While we strongly endorse the continuous development of morphological expertise, such measures alone cannot resolve the challenge of documenting cryptic diversity, given that these lineages are, inherently, morphologically indistinguishable. Contrary to the claims of Davinack and Fitzhugh (2026), our proposal (Vivien et al., 2025) does not relax systematic standards; instead, it redefines them within a framework specifically adapted to molecularly revealed diversity.
